title: Sorption Molecular Dynamics of Point Defects in 2D Materials with a Machine Learning Potential
authors: Nils-Ruben Skogemyr, Albin Sjöstedt, Isak Wernroth, Isak Häggqvist, Isac Ljungwald, Hans-Ove Åkesson
abstract: Defect engineering is a crucial tool for tuning and tailoring the properties of two-dimensional (2D) materials. A key challenge is identifying which defects are kinetically stable at room temperature and sufficiently promising to warrant further investigation. However, identifying stable defects with suitable properties using first-principles calculations, such as density functional theory (DFT) is computationally demanding, effectively limiting the scope of high-throughput studies. In this work, we investigate whether the machine learning interatomic potential MACE can reproduce sorption trends (adsorption vs. absorption) previously obtained from high-throughput DFT calculations and extend the analysis to elevated temperatures. A total of 17,624 defect structures from the ADAQ database are simulated using MACE-accelerated molecular dynamics (MD) at both 0 K and 300 K. The results show that MACE successfully reproduces the overall sorption trends observed in DFT calculations at 0 K at a fraction of the computational cost. Simulations performed at 300 K further indicate that the qualitative sorption trends remain largely the same when including finite-temperature effects. These findings demonstrate that MACE-driven MD can be used as an effective high-throughput prescreening tool for defect-related studies in 2D materials, specially related to sorption. While conventional first-principles methods, such as DFT, remain necessary for accurate and quantitative validation, the use of MLIPs enables MD simulations of finite-temperature defect behavior at a fraction of the computational cost of DFT-based MD.

infographic.key_insight: MACE-based molecular dynamics can reproduce DFT sorption trends for point defects in 2D materials and appears robust even at 300 K.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables much faster high-throughput prescreening of defect stability and sorption behavior, reducing reliance on expensive DFT-only workflows.
method: Simulated 17,624 defect structures from the ADAQ database.
Ran MACE-accelerated MD at 0 K and 300 K.
Compared adsorption vs. absorption trends against prior high-throughput DFT results.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 17,624 defect structures, MACE reproduced the overall DFT sorption trends at 0 K and showed similar qualitative trends at 300 K.
infographic.watch_item: MACE is best used for prescreening; DFT is still needed for accurate quantitative validation and final defect ranking.
infographic.paper_title: Sorption Molecular Dynamics of Point Defects in 2D Materials with a Machine Learning Potential

title: Theoretical Investigation of Oxygen-Vacancy Diffusion in SrTiO$_3$ using Neural Network Potentials
authors: Kazutaka Nishiguchi, Ryota Yamamoto, Seiichiro Ten-no
abstract: Oxygen-vacancy formation and diffusion play important roles in determining the electronic and atomic transport properties of SrTiO$_3$ (STO). Accurate analysis of such point defects requires sufficiently large-scale and long-time molecular dynamics (MD) simulations; however, direct investigations of oxygen-vacancy dynamics using {\it ab initio} MD (AIMD) based on density functional theory (DFT) are limited to relatively small systems and short time scales because of their high computational cost. In this study, we develop a neural network potential (NNP) for pristine and oxygen-deficient STO using a reference dataset generated from AIMD simulations. The trained NNP model accurately reproduces the DFT reference energies, atomic forces, and virials for both pristine STO and STO containing an oxygen vacancy. The NNP also reproduces the supercell-size dependence of the total energies and oxygen-vacancy formation energies, including the formation energy extrapolated to the dilute limit. Large-scale and long-time MD simulations using the NNP (NNP-MD) are then performed to investigate oxygen-vacancy diffusion. The resulting oxygen-vacancy diffusion coefficients show substantially better agreement with experimental data than those obtained from conventional classical MD simulations. An Arrhenius analysis yields an oxygen-vacancy migration enthalpy of 0.64 eV, in close agreement with the experimental value of 0.67 eV. These results demonstrate that NNPs trained on first-principles data provide an accurate and computationally efficient framework for investigating defect formation and long-time vacancy transport in perovskite oxides.

infographic.key_insight: A neural network potential trained on DFT data can accurately capture oxygen-vacancy energetics and long-time diffusion in SrTiO3, enabling vacancy transport studies beyond the reach of direct ab initio MD.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a fast, first-principles-based modeling route for predicting defect behavior in perovskite oxides relevant to ionic conduction, reliability, and electronic transport design.
method: Trained an NNP on AIMD/DFT reference data for pristine and oxygen-deficient SrTiO3.
Validated the NNP against DFT energies, forces, virials, and vacancy formation energies across supercell sizes.
Used large-scale NNP-MD and Arrhenius analysis to estimate vacancy diffusion and migration enthalpy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The NNP reproduces DFT reference properties and yields an oxygen-vacancy migration enthalpy of 0.64 eV, close to the experimental 0.67 eV.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on the coverage of the AIMD training set, so rare defect environments or extreme temperatures may require additional reference data.
infographic.paper_title: Theoretical Investigation of Oxygen-Vacancy Diffusion in SrTiO$_3$ using Neural Network Potentials

title: What Do Foundation Models for Market Microstructure Learn? A Controlled Study with Synthetic Limit Order Books
authors: Fernando Acero
abstract: Autoregressive transformers trained on limit order book (LOB) message streams are increasingly proposed as foundation models for market microstructure. Because the generative process of real markets is unknown, these models can be judged only by the realism of their output, leaving open what they actually learn. We make the question answerable by inverting the setup: we train GPT-style models on order flow from simulators whose latent parameters are known, so that the Bayes-optimal predictor, the generating state, and the exact data entropy serve as references. Measured against them, next-token pretraining on order flow implements amortized Bayesian inference over market regimes. The learned predictive matches the exact Bayes optimum to within a millinat per token and approaches the oracle floor even on a nonstationary family whose latent state drifts within an episode, a regime that requires filtering. The latent regime is linearly decodable from frozen activations, well above baselines, so a frozen-model read-out calibrates simulator parameters more accurately than windowed maximum likelihood at a fraction of the cost. In our experiments these capabilities are not produced by scale: capacity and token volume saturate early, and it is the diversity of training regimes, not the token count, that determines generalization to unseen markets. On real NASDAQ data, zero-shot transfer is set by how well the simulator prior covers real flow: an enriched mixture nearly closes the gap to an in-domain baseline, and pretraining beats from-scratch training at every budget across held-out tickers. Known ground truth turns average next-token loss, which is uninformative near the entropy floor, into an exact comparison against the Bayes-optimal and oracle predictors.

infographic.key_insight: Training GPT-style models on synthetic limit order book streams reveals that they learn amortized Bayesian inference over market regimes, not just next-token statistics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study shows foundation-model pretraining can recover latent simulator parameters and transfer to real NASDAQ order flow, suggesting a path to more interpretable and data-efficient market microstructure models.
method: Train autoregressive transformers on synthetic order-flow sequences from simulators with known latent states.
Benchmark predictions against exact Bayes-optimal and oracle predictors using entropy-aware evaluation.
Probe frozen activations with linear readouts to decode latent regimes and test zero-shot transfer to real data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model’s next-token predictions match the exact Bayes optimum to within a millinat per token, latent regimes are linearly decodable, and enriched simulator mixtures improve zero-shot NASDAQ transfer.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend strongly on how well the simulator prior covers real market flow, so mismatch between synthetic and real regimes may limit deployment.
infographic.paper_title: What Do Foundation Models for Market Microstructure Learn? A Controlled Study with Synthetic Limit Order Books

title: Effective Graph Neural Representation of Chain Architectures of Block Copolymers Tested by Predicting RPA Instability Limits
authors: Xiyue Zhang, Yutong Wu, Yi-Xin Liu
abstract: Advances in polymer synthesis and computational modeling are expanding the block-copolymer architecture space accessible for phase-behavior design. Machine learning can accelerate this exploration, yet a common representation capable of learning across diverse chain topologies remains lacking. Here, we present a graph neural network (GNN) representation of acyclic AB multiblock architectures, tested by random-phase approximation (RPA) instability prediction. Each chain is represented as a graph, enabling a common model to learn across diverse topologies. This representation, which organizes RPA-related information, retains predictive capability when extrapolated to architectures with more blocks and demonstrates its potential for reuse across tasks through transfer to instability-wavenumber prediction. By effectively linking block-copolymer chain architecture to field-theoretic response, this graph representation not only reconstructs stability-limit curves but also provides a practical route for future self-consistent field theory exploration of ordered phase space across complex topologies.

infographic.key_insight: A graph neural network can encode diverse acyclic AB multiblock copolymer chain architectures in a single shared representation and accurately predict their RPA instability limits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a reusable machine-learning surrogate for rapidly screening block-copolymer architectures and guiding phase-behavior design beyond hand-crafted topology descriptors.
method: Represent each copolymer chain as a graph to capture chain topology across architectures.
Train a GNN on RPA-related features to predict instability limits from architecture.
Test transfer to a related task: instability-wavenumber prediction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the model reconstructs stability-limit curves and retains predictive capability when extrapolated to architectures with more blocks, indicating generalization beyond the training topology range.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may degrade for architectures or physics regimes far outside the acyclic AB multiblock space used in training, so extrapolation should be validated before design use.
infographic.paper_title: Effective Graph Neural Representation of Chain Architectures of Block Copolymers Tested by Predicting RPA Instability Limits

title: Modelling the dynamics of the martensitic transformation in Ni$_2$MnGa with machine-learning force-fields
authors: Markus E. Gruner, Yulia Klunnikova, Mike J. Bruckhoff, Konstatin P. Skokov, Olga N. Miroshkina
abstract: The martensitic transformations in stoichiometric Ni$_2$MnGa and related Heusler alloys are governed by a delicate interplay between electronic structure, magnetism, and lattice dynamics. While density functional theory (DFT) has successfully mapped the energy landscape of modulated martensites, it remains computationally prohibitive for capturing finite-temperature dynamics across relevant length and time scales. Here, we bridge this gap by constructing DFT-trained machine-learning force-fields (ML-FF) interpolated from ab initio molecular dynamics. We demonstrate that ML-FF trained on DFT data can reproduce key features of Ni$_2$MnGa, including the soft TA$_2$ phonon and a preference for nanotwinned martensites. Using classical molecular dynamics simulations, we explore the impact of adaptive nanotwinning on the austenite-martensite transition, which facilitates the dynamics of both, forward and backward transformation. We demonstrate, that the negative twin boundary energy along the entire transformations path predicted by DFT for $T=0$, supports the formation of ordered modulated martensites at finite temperatures. Our results pave the way for large-scale simulations of magnetic shape memory alloys with near-DFT accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: DFT-trained machine-learning force fields can capture the finite-temperature martensitic dynamics of Ni2MnGa, including soft phonons and nanotwinned modulated martensites.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables near-DFT-accuracy simulations of magnetic shape memory alloys over larger length and time scales, supporting alloy design for actuators and adaptive smart materials.
method: Trained machine-learning force fields on DFT ab initio molecular dynamics data.
Ran classical molecular dynamics to simulate austenite–martensite transformation dynamics.
Analyzed phonon softening and twin-boundary energetics across the transformation path.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the ML-FF reproduces the soft TA2 phonon, predicts a preference for nanotwinned martensites, and matches the DFT-predicted negative twin-boundary energy along the full T=0 transformation path.
infographic.watch_item: The force field is only as reliable as its DFT training set, so transferability to compositions, temperatures, or strain states outside the training regime should be validated.
infographic.paper_title: Modelling the dynamics of the martensitic transformation in Ni$_2$MnGa with machine-learning force-fields

title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
authors: Kun Ryu, Yeo Jin Jung, Shyue Ping Ong, Claire Donnat, Ying Shirley Meng
abstract: Automated materials discovery requires evaluating large pools of candidate configurations, with density functional theory (DFT) as a major throughput bottleneck. Pretrained machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate DFT cheaply, but their errors vary by orders of magnitude across configurations, making it difficult to decide when to trust the MLIP predictions and when to fall back to DFT. We frame this decision as a risk-controlled selection problem and solve it within a conformal risk control (CRC) framework. Each configuration is mapped from atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates to a fixed geometric descriptor, which a lightweight predictor uses to estimate an MLIP-DFT disagreement score in energy, average force, and maximum force. CRC then calibrates this score into a selection threshold for DFT labeling such that the MLIP error on the unselected configurations, which keep their MLIP labels, stays below a user-chosen fraction $α$ of the expected error. Under an identical guarantee across eight dataset-MLIP pairs, our predictor routes 7% and 14% fewer configurations to DFT at $α=0.3$ than committee baselines. Because committee disagreement overlooks errors the MLIPs share, our gains are largest when the DFT labels and MLIP training data differ in DFT functional and basis set, and narrow when the two agree. Without model access, the structure-only predictor also ranks errors as well as the target MLIP's latent representation and outperforms widely used descriptors such as Smooth Overlap of Atomic Positions (SOAP) and Atom-Centered Symmetry Functions (ACSF).

infographic.key_insight: The paper turns DFT labeling into a risk-controlled selection problem, using conformal risk control to decide which configurations can safely keep cheaper MLIP predictions and which must be sent to DFT.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives materials workflows a principled way to cut expensive DFT calls while guaranteeing that the retained MLIP predictions stay within a user-chosen error budget.
method: Encode each structure from atomic numbers and Cartesian coordinates into a fixed geometric descriptor.
Train a lightweight predictor to estimate MLIP–DFT disagreement in energy, average force, and maximum force.
Calibrate the disagreement score with conformal risk control to set a DFT-selection threshold with a user-defined risk level α.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight dataset–MLIP pairs, the method meets the same risk guarantee and routes 7%–14% fewer configurations to DFT at α=0.3 than committee baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the calibration setting and may shrink when committee methods already capture the dominant errors, especially if DFT labels and MLIP training data use the same functional and basis set.
infographic.paper_title: Risk-Controlled DFT Selection for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials

title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
authors: Seungone Kim, Jiayi Geng, Young-Jun Lee, Bo Liu, Juyoung Suk, Nicholas Lubbers
abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

infographic.key_insight: The paper finds that frontier AI agents can draft plausible-looking follow-up research papers, but none met all domain-scientist criteria for open scientific problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For AI materials science workflows, the result shows current agents are not yet reliable for autonomous hypothesis-to-paper research without strong human oversight and validation.
method: Built the "Into the Unknown" benchmark using real unpublished follow-up directions from DOE national lab scientists.
Asked nine frontier agents to generate 15 follow-up papers each across five scientific domains.
Evaluated each submission against scientist-defined conditions and an integrity check for fabricated or contradictory claims.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 135 agent-generated submissions, none satisfied all required conditions and 114 failed integrity checks, often due to unsupported claims or numbers contradicting evidence.
infographic.watch_item: The benchmark is promising, but results depend on the specific scientist-defined rubric and may not capture every form of research quality or novelty.
infographic.paper_title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems

title: Comprehensive Workflow for Uncertainty-Aware Ionic Liquid Solvent Discovery
authors: Alexander Lobo, Urvi Awasthi, Leonid Zhukov
abstract: Designing synthesizable materials with targeted properties remains one of the central objectives in materials sciences. Ionic liquids (ILs) are well suited to this goal due to their "tunability", where physical and chemical properties can be precisely customized by modifying their molecular structure, specifically by varying the combination of cations and anions. At the same time, current data-driven property models for ionic liquids often degrade in scarce, noisy, and uneven data regimes, where measurements cover only a small fraction of chemical space and a limited range of thermodynamic conditions. This makes out-of-distribution screening brittle: even when point predictions look plausible, it is difficult to compare candidates consistently, quantify downstream implications, or trust rankings enough to guide molecular discovery. We present a property-prediction and optimal candidate selection workflow that treats data processing, deep learning modeling, and physics-based calculations as a coupled system, linking property prediction with uncertainty estimation and physics-based filtering. By tightening the link between predicted properties and the criteria used for down-selection, the workflow supports reliable out-of-distribution ranking and enables prioritization of previously untested ionic liquid candidates with favorable predicted trade-offs. We demonstrate the application of our workflow by designing novel ionic liquids for CO2 capture from flue gas, predicting their properties and selecting Pareto-optimal candidates based on CO2 solubility, IL viscosity and working capacity.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes an uncertainty-aware workflow that couples deep learning, physics-based filtering, and Pareto ranking to reliably discover new ionic liquids with targeted properties.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more trustworthy out-of-distribution screening for ionic liquid design, helping engineers prioritize synthesizable candidates for CO2 capture with balanced solubility, viscosity, and working capacity.
method: Clean and process sparse, noisy ionic-liquid property data for model training.
Use deep learning with uncertainty estimation to predict properties across chemical space.
Apply physics-based calculations and Pareto-optimal selection to down-select candidates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports application to novel ionic liquids for flue-gas CO2 capture, using predicted properties and Pareto ranking to select previously untested candidates.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may still depend on the quality and coverage of scarce, uneven experimental data, so uncertainty estimates should be checked carefully before experimental follow-up.
infographic.paper_title: Comprehensive Workflow for Uncertainty-Aware Ionic Liquid Solvent Discovery

title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning
authors: Minhyuk Kang, Beom Seok Kang, Nikolai Argatoff, Miguel Nouman, Danish Khan, William A. Goddard
abstract: Accurate electronic band structures are essential for predicting material properties, but high-fidelity calculations are computationally demanding. We introduce O-kRystal, a dual-space orbital-learning framework that uses a lower-cost Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) calculation as both an energy baseline and a source of structured orbital information. Combining PBE band energies with real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices, O-kRystal predicts higher-level corrections for individual electronic states as a function of crystal momentum and spin. For states within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint, it predicts Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof (HSE06) band energies with a mean absolute error of $0.171 \pm 0.009$ eV across nearly 6,000 three-dimensional materials spanning insulating, metallic, magnetic, and nonmagnetic systems. On a separate benchmark of six strongly correlated materials, it reduces the corresponding PBE band-energy MAE by 68.7% and resolves orbital-dependent changes in the relative placement of transition-metal d and ligand p states. Despite training only at high-symmetry points, it maintains comparable accuracy at unseen points along band paths and reconstructs HSE06 densities of states from dense Brillouin-zone predictions. Finally, training O-kRystal on $G_0W_0$ quasiparticle energies for two-dimensional materials demonstrates its applicability across levels of theory and the potential of orbital learning for higher-fidelity, momentum-resolved electronic-structure prediction beyond density functional theory.

infographic.key_insight: O-kRystal learns orbital-informed corrections from cheap PBE calculations to predict higher-level band structures, achieving HSE06-level accuracy across diverse materials and even unseen k-points.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, more scalable electronic-structure screening for semiconductors, correlated materials, and 2D systems without running full high-cost calculations everywhere.
method: Uses PBE as both an energy baseline and a source of real- and reciprocal-space orbital matrices.
Predicts state-by-state corrections to band energies as functions of crystal momentum and spin.
Trained at high-symmetry points, then generalized to band paths and dense Brillouin-zone density-of-states reconstruction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across nearly 6,000 3D materials, the model predicts HSE06 band energies within 5 eV of the band-edge midpoint with 0.171 ± 0.009 eV MAE, and it also improves six strongly correlated materials by 68.7% over PBE.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy may drop for states far from the band-edge window or for systems whose orbital character differs substantially from the training distribution.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond DFT electronic band structures via dual-space orbital learning

title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning
authors: Hongrui Sheng, Shutian Liang, Reid A. Coyle, Shyam Chand Pal, Peter Walther, Bin Feng
abstract: Reticular chemistry allows metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) to be designed from their building units, yet their synthesis remains constrained by sparse experimental data, noisy crystallization outcomes, and the absence of benchmarks for comparing active-learning strategies. While data-driven approaches such as Bayesian optimization (BO) can improve synthesis success rates, selecting appropriate optimizers beforehand for mapping MOF crystallization landscapes remains largely empirical. Here we present ActMOF, an experiment-grounded benchmark for comparing search strategies in aluminum-carboxylate MOF synthesis. ActMOF is emulated from experimentally measured microwave syntheses with each encoded condition assigned a crystallinity index calculated based on diffraction peak intensity and full width at half-maximum. By benchmarking policies guided by Gaussian processes (GP), tree ensembles and large language models (LLM), ActMOF placed the GP family among the leading policies for active learning in sparse synthesis landscapes. It then demonstrated transferability by guiding the microwave synthesis of six reticularly related aluminum MOFs. All six campaigns gave crystalline products within a fixed budget of 12 experiments each, and established a reusable testbed for AI-driven MOF synthesis.

infographic.key_insight: ActMOF turns real microwave MOF synthesis data into a benchmark for testing active-learning strategies, showing that Gaussian-process-based policies work especially well in sparse crystallization search spaces.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps engineers choose and compare optimization methods before running costly experiments, improving the efficiency of reticular synthesis development.
method: Emulated experimental MOF crystallization conditions from measured microwave syntheses.
Assigned each condition a crystallinity index from diffraction peak intensity and peak width.
Benchmarked Gaussian processes, tree ensembles, and LLM-guided search policies for active learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using a fixed budget of 12 experiments per campaign, the benchmark found GP-family policies among the strongest performers and successfully transferred guidance to six related aluminum MOF syntheses, all yielding crystalline products.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the quality and representativeness of sparse experimental data, so benchmark results may not transfer uniformly across other MOF families or synthesis platforms.
infographic.paper_title: ActMOF: Mapping Reticular Synthesis through Active Learning

title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells
authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou
abstract: Existing machine-learning models for perovskite solar cells struggle to predict devices made from new materials. Most treat device layers as arbitrary categorical labels and represent perovskite absorbers either through featureless composition vectors or through rigid crystal graphs that require a pre-solved unit cell. As a result, they cannot generalize to unrecorded alloys or unfamiliar cell architectures. We present the Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System (V-PaSS), an architecture built around the physical continuity of perovskite solid solutions. V-PaSS represents arbitrary mixed-cation, mixed-halide absorbers by interpolating relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure $ABX_3$ endpoint compounds via Vegard's law with learned bandgap bowing. For the device stack, it couples layer sequence and cell polarity (n-i-p or p-i-n) with interfacial band offsets and encodes chemical descriptions with a scientific language model. Evaluated under an institution-grouped protocol where test devices come exclusively from unseen laboratories, an untuned default configuration of V-PaSS achieves the lowest error among fourteen tested models (2.861% MAE, a 5.2% relative reduction over a gradient-boosted baseline at 3.017%, and outperforming the best tuned benchmark at 2.912%). V-PaSS pulls furthest ahead where test devices differ most from training: reducing error by 15.7-19.0% on unseen absorber alloys, by 16.1% on mixed absorbers from new laboratories, and widening its lead over the baseline by 3.6$\times$ on devices with unobserved transport layers. Combined with tree ensembles, V-PaSS sets a new state of the art across all five benchmark splits.

infographic.key_insight: V-PaSS improves perovskite solar-cell prediction by representing mixed compositions as physically interpolated “virtual alloys” instead of treating new materials as unrelated categories.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes extrapolative device screening more reliable for novel absorber alloys, new transport layers, and unseen laboratory settings, which is critical for accelerating perovskite design and scale-up.
method: Interpolates relaxed crystal graphs of 23 pure ABX3 endpoints using Vegard’s law plus learned bandgap bowing.
Encodes device stacks with layer order, polarity (n-i-p or p-i-n), and interfacial band offsets.
Uses a scientific language model to convert chemical descriptions into semantic features.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under an institution-grouped evaluation with unseen laboratories in test data, V-PaSS achieved 2.861% MAE, outperforming 14 compared models and showing the largest gains on unseen alloys and unfamiliar device components.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on endpoint crystal graphs, learned bowing parameters, and good interfacial descriptors, so performance may drop if those physical inputs are incomplete or noisy.
infographic.paper_title: Virtual-Alloy Physics-Aware Semantic System for extrapolative prediction of perovskite solar cells

title: Accurately Generalizing Deep-Learning Hamiltonian Methods to Plane-Wave Density Functional Theory
authors: Chuntian Wu, Jiaxiang Li, Qiang Xu, Xuecheng Shao, Congwei Xie, Yu Xie
abstract: Deep neural networks that predict density functional theory (DFT) Hamiltonians from material structures offer a route to efficient electronic-structure calculations. However, extending localized atomic-orbital (AO) Hamiltonian learning to plane-wave (PW) calculations with hybrid functionals requires a compact AO representation that preserves the effects of nonlocal operators. Here we propose a projectability-guided construction of nonorthogonal AO Hamiltonians from a small, selected set of PW eigenstates and eigenvalues. High-projectability states are retained, and selected higher-energy states complete the AO subspace, avoiding an empirical shift and its arbitrary contribution to the learning targets. Because the construction uses PW eigenstates and eigenvalues, it incorporates nonlocal contributions present in the reference calculation without explicitly reconstructing their AO matrix elements. Benchmarks for MoS2 and sodium phases show accurate reproduction of PW bands with smaller AO bases than real-space reconstruction. The resulting PBE and HSE Hamiltonians can be learned by equivariant neural networks, connecting PW reference calculations with electronic-structure prediction. This approach broadens the range of PW DFT calculations available for AO Hamiltonian learning and enables compact, accurate training targets for developing more widely applicable electronic-structure models.

infographic.key_insight: A projectability-guided AO construction can turn plane-wave DFT outputs into compact Hamiltonian learning targets while preserving nonlocal hybrid-functional effects.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables accurate, smaller-basis training data for neural-network Hamiltonian models, making plane-wave DFT workflows more practical for scalable electronic-structure prediction.
method: Select high-projectability PW eigenstates as the core AO subspace.
Add selected higher-energy states to complete the subspace without using an empirical shift.
Build nonorthogonal AO Hamiltonians directly from PW eigenvalues and eigenstates, retaining nonlocal operator contributions implicitly.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks on MoS2 and sodium phases show the constructed PBE and HSE Hamiltonians reproduce PW band structures accurately with smaller AO bases than real-space reconstruction.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on careful state selection and projectability thresholds, so robustness may vary across materials with different band entanglement or basis requirements.
infographic.paper_title: Accurately Generalizing Deep-Learning Hamiltonian Methods to Plane-Wave Density Functional Theory

title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites
authors: Simone Grillo, Offir Zachs Maishlos, Liya Koren, Rotem Strassberg, Rachel Lifer, Edi Maizenberg
abstract: Double perovskites (DPs) offer a compositionally versatile platform for photocatalysis and optoelectronics, but their soft lattices favor strong exciton-phonon coupling and self-trapped excitons (STEs), which produce broad, red-shifted photoluminescence (PL). Here, we combine optical spectroscopy and ab initio calculations to study lead-free, Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals with B-site alloying from Na to K. Alloying tunes the PL energy from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV, while absorption features near 3.8 eV remain nearly unchanged. Calculations reveal that Sb doping enables bright radiative recombination channels and delocalizes the excitonic wavefunction. We identify STEs responsible for the large PL red shift, associated with an upward shift of dopant-hybridized in-gap states. Na-to-K substitution selectively changes the STE lattice distortion, explaining why PL varies strongly with composition while absorption does not. Theory further predicts pronounced PL polarization anisotropy that reflects the STE wavefunction's spatial structure and depends on B-site composition. Time-resolved anisotropy measurements closely agree with these predictions, providing experimental fingerprints of the excitonic wavefunction and its evolution with alloying. Together, these results disentangle the roles of doping and alloying in lead-free DPs and establish polarization-resolved spectroscopy as a probe of STE wavefunctions.

infographic.key_insight: Sb doping creates bright, self-trapped exciton emission in Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals, while Na-to-K alloying tunes the exciton lattice distortion and shifts photoluminescence energy without strongly changing absorption.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These lead-free double perovskites offer composition-tunable optical fingerprints for safer optoelectronic materials, with polarization-resolved emission providing a practical handle to probe and optimize excitonic behavior.
method: Optical spectroscopy of Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals across B-site alloying from Na to K
Ab initio calculations of excitonic states, lattice distortion, and radiative pathways
Time-resolved anisotropy measurements to test predicted PL polarization fingerprints
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments and theory show PL shifts from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV while absorption near 3.8 eV stays nearly unchanged, and measured anisotropy matches the predicted composition-dependent STE fingerprints.
infographic.watch_item: The strong STE response depends on soft-lattice composition, so device performance may be sensitive to exact alloying, defect levels, and nanocrystal synthesis control.
infographic.paper_title: Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites

title: Learning from fracture: Teaching language models to design through physical experience
authors: Bo Ni
abstract: How can language models learn to optimize physical designs through experience? We introduce FracLearn, an experience-abstraction-generalization framework evaluated through a deliberately unfamiliar, Tetris-inspired fracture game. The model first proposes architectures and examines simulated fracture responses to accumulate experience. Abstraction organizes these observations into conditional principles linking reinforcement placement, crack evolution and load transfer, with supporting evidence and failure conditions. Generalization challenges the model to combine these principles in new architectures and surpass the earlier design record. Campaigns demonstrate progressive refinement and recovery through hypothesis revision, yielding a best composite score 11.0% above the experience-stage record. Fracture analyses connect improved performance to crack deflection and temporary trapping as toughening mechanisms, alongside greater residual load capacity. Learning occurs through external knowledge and decisions, without model-weight updates. This approach offers a route to scientific agents that turn computational experiments into reusable physical knowledge for materials discovery and engineering design.

infographic.key_insight: FracLearn teaches a language model to improve physical design by converting simulated fracture experiences into reusable design principles, then applying them to new architectures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a path to AI copilots for materials and structural design that learn from experiments and transfer hard-won physical knowledge without retraining model weights.
method: Generate candidate architectures for a fracture game and observe simulated responses.
Abstract experience into conditional rules linking reinforcement placement, crack evolution, and load transfer.
Generalize by recombining learned rules on new designs to surpass prior records.
infographic.evidence_signal: In campaigns, the model achieved a best composite score 11.0% above the experience-stage record, with fracture analyses attributing gains to crack deflection, temporary trapping, and higher residual load capacity.
infographic.watch_item: The framework was tested in a deliberately unfamiliar, game-like setting, so transfer to real materials and manufacturing constraints still needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Learning from fracture: Teaching language models to design through physical experience

title: Sounds Cheesy - Bridging the Texture Gap Between Dairy and Plant-Based cheese with Non-Contact Ultrasound and AI
authors: Wenjing Feng, Thomas A. Hazlehurst, Nik Watson
abstract: Plant-based cheeses often fail to reproduce the texture of dairy cheese. Closing this gap is slow because the reference methods, texture profile analysis (TPA) and sensory panels, destroy the sample and are poorly suited to screening many formulations in a timely and cost-effective manner. Here we show that non-contact, air-coupled ultrasonic imaging combined with machine learning can characterise cheese texture rapidly and without damaging the sample. Thirteen commercial products (nine dairy, four plant-based; 119 slices, 357 scans) were imaged in through-transmission at 100 kHz to give two-channel amplitude and time-of-flight C-scans, and each slice was then measured by TPA. The C-scans revealed millimetre-scale acoustic domains in ripened dairy cheeses, consistent with their fused-curd microstructure, that were absent from the homogeneous starch and oil matrix of the plant-based products. TPA showed that the texture gap is one of range and failure behaviour rather than average firmness. Mean hardness was similar for the two categories, but dairy products spanned a 7.5-fold range against 1.9-fold for plant-based products, and the plant-based products failed in a brittle, strain-softening manner rather than by ductile yielding. No single ultrasonic parameter tracked texture across products. However, a compact convolutional neural network predicted full true stress-strain loading and unloading curves from the C-scan images of unseen slices across all thirteen products without product-specific calibration. Clustering the predicted curves produced a texture map on which three plant-based slices sat with the Cheddars and one with Emmental, while soft, mozzarella-like textures remained unoccupied. The approach offers a one-minute, non-contact measurement suited to formulation screening and at-line quality control of cheese.

infographic.key_insight: Non-contact air-coupled ultrasound plus AI can infer full cheese texture behavior from images, closing part of the measurement gap between dairy and plant-based cheeses without destroying the sample.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables rapid, one-minute, at-line screening of formulations and quality control for texture optimization in food materials discovery.
method: Imaged 13 commercial cheeses with through-transmission air-coupled ultrasound at 100 kHz.
Converted scans into paired amplitude and time-of-flight C-scan images.
Trained a compact CNN to predict full true stress-strain curves from unseen slices.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study used 119 slices and 357 scans, and the model generalized across all 13 products without product-specific calibration.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was demonstrated on a limited set of commercial cheeses, so broader validation is needed before routine industrial deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Sounds Cheesy - Bridging the Texture Gap Between Dairy and Plant-Based cheese with Non-Contact Ultrasound and AI

title: Learning When to Transfer: Reinforcement Learning for Carbon-Footprint Modeling in New Manufacturing Domains
authors: Muhammad Umar Farooq, Daniel R. Cooper
abstract: Manufacturers often need to characterize a new material, process, or product before enough operating data are available to train reliable predictive models for this new, target domain. Existing manufacturing operations contain potentially useful knowledge to accelerate this characterization, but indiscriminate reuse of data from existing source domains can cause negative transfer in learning of the new, target domain when the manufacturing domains differ sufficiently. This work proposes a reinforcement-learning method for selective knowledge transfer, where its reward scores each opportunity to transfer against supervised alternatives, so negative transfer is avoided and controlled during forward prediction instead of being diagnosed afterwards. Given limited data from a new target domain, the learned policy chooses among predictors based on individual source operations, subsets of the sources, or the supervised alternatives: fully pooled sources, or target data alone. A validation gate deploys the transferred prediction only when it improves upon the supervised alternatives. The method is designed for learning variables supporting carbon accounting, as well as performance and quality outcomes. We demonstrate the approach by quantifying the embodied greenhouse-gas emissions of parts produced via material-extrusion additive manufacturing, using data from 729 experiments spanning five materials: ABS, PETG, TPU, PLA, and recycled PLA. The response combines measured fabrication electricity with polymer-specific cradle-to-gate production factors, while 22 material, process, and toolpath features characterize each experiment. In leave-one-material-out evaluation, this method achieves a mean test RMSE of 5.2 g CO2e per part, 20.00% lower than target-only training (32.5% lower when only 5-10% of the target training data are available) and 10.30% lower than indiscriminate source-target pooling.

infographic.key_insight: A reinforcement-learning policy learns when to transfer knowledge from prior manufacturing domains, avoiding negative transfer while improving carbon-footprint prediction in a new target domain.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method helps manufacturers estimate embodied emissions earlier with limited data, supporting faster decision-making for sustainable process and product design.
method: Learns a transfer policy that selects among source-specific models, subsets of sources, pooled sources, or target-only prediction.
Uses a validation gate to deploy transferred predictions only when they beat supervised alternatives.
Designed to predict carbon-accounting variables and other performance/quality outcomes from limited new-domain data.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on 729 material-extrusion 3D-printing experiments across five polymers, with leave-one-material-out testing; mean test RMSE was 5.2 g CO2e per part, outperforming target-only training and source-target pooling.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on having representative source domains and careful validation gating; poorly matched sources can still cause negative transfer if the policy is not well trained.
infographic.paper_title: Learning When to Transfer: Reinforcement Learning for Carbon-Footprint Modeling in New Manufacturing Domains

title: Ionic gradients shape the spatial organization and dynamics of supramolecular polymers
authors: Claudio Perego, Annalisa Cardellini, Andrea Tagliabue, Giovanni M. Pavan
abstract: Living supramolecular materials such as microtubules and actin filaments assemble and function in dynamic, heterogeneous environments, subject to chemical concentration gradients. Their rapid and precise response to such gradients---via aggregation, disassembly, or autonomous motion---underlies the fine spatiotemporal control typical of living systems. Reproducing such responsiveness in synthetic materials is a central challenge in materials science and requires a molecular-level understanding of how gradients couple to supramolecular structure and dynamics, which remains difficult to access experimentally. To this end, we combine implicit-solvent coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MD) with the constant chemical potential MD (C$μ$MD) technique to investigate, at molecular resolution, the coupling of two prototypical supramolecular polymer models with externally imposed ionic concentration gradients. Despite their contrasting responses to homogeneous ionic conditions, both systems undergo pronounced spatial reorganization under the gradient, generating regions of locally enhanced supramolecular activity that are inaccessible to homogeneous systems with the same overall content of self-assembling species. Crucially, the local supramolecular dynamics is largely determined by the local concentrations, consistent with the formation of local quasi-equilibria: this direct connection between spatial composition and supramolecular activity emerges as a common governing principle across the two models. These findings shed light on the spatially complex supramolecular response that can be triggered by chemical gradients, and show how a single gradient simulation can encode this response across a continuous range of local chemical environments, thus providing a general strategy to investigate and design materials operating under spatially heterogeneous conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Ionic concentration gradients reorganize supramolecular polymers into spatially distinct zones where local composition directly controls local assembly dynamics, creating quasi-equilibrium behavior across the gradient.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests gradients can be used as a design knob to program where synthetic soft materials assemble, disassemble, or become dynamically active in space and time.
method: Implicit-solvent coarse-grained molecular dynamics
Constant chemical potential molecular dynamics (CμMD)
Two prototypical supramolecular polymer models under imposed ionic gradients
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports molecular-resolution simulations showing pronounced spatial reorganization and locally enhanced supramolecular activity under gradients, with local dynamics largely matching local concentrations.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusion is based on simulation models, so translation to real materials will depend on whether the coarse-grained interactions and imposed gradient conditions faithfully capture experimental systems.
infographic.paper_title: Ionic gradients shape the spatial organization and dynamics of supramolecular polymers

title: Knowledge-Guided Construction of Machine Learning Potentials for Reactive Behavior in Energetic Materials
authors: Guanchen Dong, Huanrong Liu, Lin Wang, Yuxuan Chen, Zhengyu Tu, Qing-an Li
abstract: Energetic materials involve multiple interactions, making reliable machine-learning potentials (MLPs) difficult to construct without extensive datasets. Here, we enhance the ability of the neural network interatomic potential (NNAP) to describe molecular systems using sphmulti, a refined spherical-harmonic basis set that combines extra radial basis with element-specific chemical weighting in each radial channel. We further integrate hyperactive learning, farthest-point sampling, and iterative sufficiency criteria with knowledge-guided key events, enabling the NNAP to retain essential information for describing the material system. For 3,3'-diamino-4,4'-azoxyfurazan, the resulting NNAP is trained on only 13,680 configurations yet captures key properties, including the isomerization barrier, pyrolysis activation energy, and shock Hugoniot behavior. NNAP-driven molecular dynamics simulations further reveal that pyrolysis proceeds through furazan-ring opening followed by chain reactions, whereas shock loading induces anisotropic hydrogen transfer driven by interlayer structural deformations. This work enables efficient and reliable MLPs for energetic materials.

infographic.key_insight: A knowledge-guided training strategy can make a neural-network interatomic potential accurate for reactive energetic materials while using far fewer configurations than conventional data-hungry approaches.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, more reliable molecular simulation of pyrolysis and shock response in energetic materials, supporting safer materials design and screening.
method: Enhance NNAP with sphmulti: refined spherical-harmonic basis, extra radial basis, and element-specific chemical weighting.
Combine hyperactive learning, farthest-point sampling, and iterative sufficiency criteria to prioritize informative configurations.
Inject knowledge-guided key events so the model preserves critical reactive pathways during training.
infographic.evidence_signal: The NNAP was trained on only 13,680 configurations yet reproduced the isomerization barrier, pyrolysis activation energy, and shock Hugoniot behavior for 3,3'-diamino-4,4'-azoxyfurazan.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on identifying representative key events and sufficient sampling, so performance may drop if rare reactive pathways or loading conditions are missed.
infographic.paper_title: Knowledge-Guided Construction of Machine Learning Potentials for Reactive Behavior in Energetic Materials

title: Trust-Limited Machine-Learning-Accelerated Nudged Elastic Band Calculations for Small-Polaron Hopping in Rutile TiO2
authors: Ashish Kumar Singh, Irina V. Lebedeva
abstract: Nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations of small-polaron hopping are demanding because nuclear motion is coupled to a self-consistent localized electronic state. Near the charge-transfer region, slow self-consistent-field convergence, localization switching, and competing electronic solutions complicate surrogate-assisted optimization. We develop a Gaussian-process-assisted NEB workflow for this regime and demonstrate electron small-polaron hopping in rutile TiO2 using spin-polarized density functional theory with a Hubbard U correction (DFT+U ) with SIESTA. A joint energy-force Gaussian process (GP) with a Matérn covariance model advances the elastic band, while active-atom root-mean-square and maximum-atom displacement limits constrain surrogate motion relative to evaluated configurations. Reaching these limits triggers first-principles sampling without requiring full surrogate convergence. Three independently DFT-verified 96-atom [001] calculations using 11, 13, and 15 images and different surrogate settings and GP parameterizations yield barriers of 0.1645, 0.1637, and 0.1640 eV, respectively, spanning 0.793 meV. In the 15-image calculation, repeated central-image sampling activates a separately calibrated local GP during surrogate optimization. Final full-band DFT verification gives a maximum projected NEB force of 0.0346 eV/Å. A 324-atom calculation yields a lower barrier of 0.1302 eV, indicating supercell sensitivity and demonstrating feasibility at larger GP observation dimension. The workflow combines controlled surrogate extrapolation, targeted charge-transfer-region interpolation, and independent DFT verification to obtain polaron migration pathways, emphasizing reproducible barriers and full-band force convergence.

infographic.key_insight: A trust-limited Gaussian-process surrogate can accelerate NEB path searches for polaron hopping while staying anchored to DFT-verified configurations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more reproducible migration-barrier calculations for defect and ion-transport studies in complex materials where self-consistent electronic localization makes standard NEB expensive.
method: Joint energy-force Gaussian process with Matérn covariance guides elastic-band updates.
Active-atom RMS and max-displacement trust limits trigger new first-principles samples before surrogate drift.
Independent full-band DFT verification is used to confirm the final NEB path and forces.
infographic.evidence_signal: Three 96-atom DFT-verified runs with 11, 13, and 15 images produced consistent barriers of 0.1645, 0.1637, and 0.1640 eV, and a 324-atom run gave 0.1302 eV.
infographic.watch_item: Results are sensitive to supercell size and charge-transfer-region localization switching, so surrogate settings and verification steps must be carefully calibrated.
infographic.paper_title: Trust-Limited Machine-Learning-Accelerated Nudged Elastic Band Calculations for Small-Polaron Hopping in Rutile TiO2

title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
authors: Delip Rao, Ahmed Muharram, Chris Callison-Burch
abstract: Co-scientists and agentic scientific claim verifiers are increasingly used to assess claims across the sciences. Natural-language scientific claims, written for human experts, are often underspecified and so admit several defensible interpretations. Such verifiers usually pick one, often tacitly, and benchmarks score their verdicts against expert labels without recording the expert's interpretation or the verifier's in a comparable form. This leads to disagreements with expert labels that cannot be traced to the evidence or the interpretation, and to compute spent on unchecked interpretations. We introduce Claim Cards to make such interpretations explicit in the reasoning itself. A Claim Card records a verifier's interpretation as nine fields before evidence gathering, each marked stated, inferred, or default. To test whether an agent's interpretation can change its verdict, we ran a GPT-5.4 agent five times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims with a card, without one, and with one card frozen across runs (900 runs). Over 40% of card fields were not marked stated, and a card added about a tenth to a run's GPT-5.4 tokens and time without measurably changing agreement with expert labels. The agent's own interpretations varied between runs, although within a claim this variation did not measurably track the verdict. A deliberate change to one field of the frozen card, however, making the quantifier universal or the threshold for support stricter, changed the verdict on about a third of the claims, against about one in seven expected by chance (p < 0.001 for each edit). On 24 materials-science claims run with computational tools, the stricter threshold also changed what the agent asked those tools to compute. We therefore argue that verdicts should be reported with their interpretations and that benchmarks could publish the interpretation behind each label.

infographic.key_insight: LLM scientific claim verifiers can reach the same verdict for different underlying interpretations, so the interpretation itself should be made explicit alongside the label.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For AI materials-science workflows, exposing and tracking claim interpretations can improve auditability, reproducibility, and tool-use decisions in automated literature verification.
method: Built a 9-field Claim Card to record a verifier’s interpretation before evidence gathering, marking each field as stated, inferred, or default.
Ran a GPT-5.4 agent 5 times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims in three settings: with a card, without a card, and with a frozen card.
Tested how deliberate edits to one frozen-card field (quantifier/threshold) changed verdicts and, for 24 materials-science claims, downstream computational tool queries.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 900 runs, over 40% of card fields were not stated, and adding a card increased GPT-5.4 tokens and time by about 10% without measurably changing agreement with expert labels; changing one interpretation field altered verdicts on about one-third of claims.
infographic.watch_item: The study uses one agent setup and a modest claim set, so results may not generalize to other models, domains, or benchmark annotation practices.
infographic.paper_title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
